data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 11 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatomyositis** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define dermatomyositis (DM).**
- Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin lesions and proximal symmetrical muscle weakness; part of the IIM group (with polymyositis, inclusion body myositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome)
- Bimodal: juvenile (5–15 y) and adult (40–60 y), women 2:1

**Q2. Classify dermatomyositis (Bohan & Peter / Sontheimer).**
- Classic adult DM, juvenile DM, cancer-associated DM, DM overlapping with other CTD
- Clinically amyopathic DM (CADM): skin signs ≥6 months without weakness — amyopathic (normal muscle tests) and hypomyopathic (subclinical abnormal tests)
- Polymyositis (no skin), inclusion body myositis

**Q3. Describe the pathognomonic and characteristic skin signs (Gottron's — PYQ).**
- Pathognomonic: Gottron's papules (violaceous flat-topped papules over knuckles — MCP, PIP, DIP joints) and Gottron's sign (violaceous macules/patches over extensor surfaces of joints — elbows, knees, knuckles, malleoli)
- Characteristic: heliotrope rash (violet-purple erythema ± oedema of upper eyelids), periungual telangiectasia with cuticular overgrowth and haemorrhages (ragged cuticles — Samitz sign), poikiloderma of photo-exposed areas — V-sign (anterior neck/chest), shawl sign (back and shoulders), holster sign (lateral thighs)
- Others: scalp erythema with scaling and non-scarring alopecia, mechanic's hands (hyperkeratotic fissured lateral fingers — antisynthetase syndrome), calcinosis cutis (juvenile), flagellate erythema, Raynaud's, ulcers (MDA5), panniculitis, vasculitis, pruritus (more than in lupus — helps differentiate)

**Q4. Describe the muscle involvement.**
- Proximal symmetrical weakness of shoulder and hip girdles (difficulty combing hair, rising from squatting, climbing stairs), neck flexors, pharyngeal muscles (dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, aspiration), respiratory muscles; myalgia; distal and facial muscles spared

**Q5. Myositis-specific autoantibodies and their associations.**
- Anti-Mi-2: classic DM, prominent skin, good response, low cancer risk
- Anti-TIF1γ (p155/140): strong association with malignancy in adults; severe skin, 'red on white' lesions, palmar hyperkeratotic papules
- Anti-NXP2: calcinosis in juvenile DM, adult malignancy, oedema
- Anti-MDA5 (CADM-140): clinically amyopathic DM, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (high mortality — especially in Asians), palmar papules (inverse Gottron's), skin ulcers, arthritis
- Anti-SAE: skin first then muscle, dysphagia
- Antisynthetase (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ): myositis, ILD, mechanic's hands, arthritis, Raynaud's, fever

**Q6. How do you investigate DM?**
- Muscle enzymes: CK (most sensitive), aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT; may be normal in CADM
- EMG (myopathic pattern: short polyphasic potentials, fibrillation), MRI of thighs (oedema on STIR — guides biopsy), muscle biopsy (perifascicular atrophy, perivascular inflammation, MxA expression)
- Skin biopsy: interface dermatitis with dermal mucin (similar to lupus); DIF usually negative (unlike lupus)
- ANA, myositis-specific/associated antibody panel
- ILD screen: HRCT chest, PFTs (DLCO); ECG/echo for cardiac; barium swallow/manometry for dysphagia
- Cancer screening in adults (especially first 3 years): CBC, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis, ovarian (CA-125, pelvic USG), breast, colorectal, nasopharyngeal (in Asians), PSA; repeat annually for 3 years

**Q7. Which malignancies are associated with DM?**
- 15–25% of adult DM; ovarian, lung, breast, stomach, colorectal, pancreatic, nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Southeast Asia/China), lymphoma
- Risk factors: age >45–50, male, TIF1γ/NXP2 antibodies, rapid onset, cutaneous necrosis/ulcers, dysphagia, normal CK, poor treatment response

**Q8. Juvenile DM — differences from adult.**
- More vasculopathy (ulceration, lipodystrophy, GI vasculitis), calcinosis (up to 40%), no malignancy association, better prognosis; treat aggressively early (methotrexate + steroids) to prevent calcinosis

**Q9. Differentiate DM from SLE skin disease.**
- DM: violaceous, itchy, over knuckles (Gottron's), heliotrope, scalp involvement, shawl/V sign poikiloderma, periungual changes, muscle weakness, raised CK
- SLE: pink-red, less itchy, between knuckles (spares joints), malar rash spares nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, ANA/anti-dsDNA, DIF lupus band positive

**Q10. Management of DM.**
- Photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen), physiotherapy, speech therapy for dysphagia
- Systemic corticosteroids prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone pulse for severe) tapered over months
- Steroid-sparing from the start: methotrexate 15–25 mg/week, azathioprine, mycophenolate (also for ILD)
- Skin: topical steroids/tacrolimus, hydroxychloroquine (watch drug rash — common in DM), methotrexate, dapsone, IVIG (very effective for skin and muscle — approved for DM), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib — refractory skin and MDA5-ILD)
- Refractory: IVIG, rituximab, cyclophosphamide/tacrolimus (ILD), cyclosporine
- Calcinosis: diltiazem, bisphosphonates, probenecid, sodium thiosulphate (topical/intralesional/IV), surgical excision
- Treat underlying malignancy (DM may remit)

**Q11. Prognosis.**
- 5-year survival ~70–90%; worse with malignancy, ILD (MDA5), dysphagia/aspiration, cardiac involvement, older age, delayed treatment

## Quick spotter facts
- Gottron's papules over knuckles + heliotrope eyelids — dermatomyositis
- Anti-MDA5 — rapidly progressive ILD; anti-TIF1γ — cancer
- Screen for malignancy in adults

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermatomyositis); 2017 EULAR/ACR idiopathic inflammatory myopathy criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
